paraphrase: Chapter 13 (in this edition 35 verses; 34 in the 700-verse numbering) distinguishes the field (kṣetra) from its knower (kṣetrajña). Movements: Arjuna asks about prakṛti and puruṣa, field and knower, knowledge and the knowable (13.1, only in editions with the extra verse). The body is the field and whoever knows it is its knower; the Lord is the knower in all fields, and knowing field and knower is knowledge (13.2-13.3). The subject is announced as sung by the seers and in the brahma-sūtra words (13.4-13.5). The field is enumerated: elements, the sense of 'I', understanding, the unmanifest, the faculties and their objects, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain and others (13.6-13.7). Twenty dispositions, from absence of pride to seeing the aim of the knowledge of reality, are called knowledge; the rest is ignorance (13.8-13.12). The knowable is the beginningless highest brahman, neither being nor non-being, described by paradox as everywhere and nowhere confined, the light of lights seated in the heart (13.13-13.18); the Lord's devotee who understands this comes to his state (13.19). Prakṛti and puruṣa are both beginningless; prakṛti is the cause of agency, puruṣa of experiencing; attachment to the guṇas causes births; the highest person in the body is onlooker, sustainer and supreme self; whoever knows this is not born again (13.20-13.24). People see the self by meditation, by sāṃkhya, by the yoga of action, or worship after hearing from others (13.25-13.26). Every being arises from the union of field and knower; the one who sees the Lord equally in all, sees prakṛti as the doer and oneself as not the doer, and sees the manifold as resting in the one, sees truly and reaches brahman (13.27-13.31). The beginningless supreme self does not act and is not stained, like space; it illumines the field as the sun the world (13.32-13.34). Those who know the difference of field and knower with the eye of knowledge go to the highest (13.35).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Chapter purpose as the chapter states it: knowledge of the field and its knower is knowledge (13.3), and knowing their difference leads to the highest (13.35). Verse refs in this edition's numbering (one higher than the 700-verse numbering from 13.2 on).

kṣetrakṣetrajñayorjñānaṃ yattajjñānaṃ mataṃ mama

Desire, aversion, pleasure and pain are here listed among the contents of the field, not of its knower.

paraphrase: Chapter 14 (27 verses) sets out the three guṇas and the way beyond them. Movements: the Lord announces again the highest knowledge, by which sages reached perfection and are not reborn at creation nor troubled at dissolution (14.1-14.2). Great brahman is his womb, in which he places the germ; he is the seed-giving father of all forms (14.3-14.4). Sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakṛti, bind the embodied one: sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas by attachment to action, tamas by heedlessness, indolence and sleep (14.5-14.9). Each prevails by overpowering the others, and each has its signs: light and knowledge; greed, activity and restlessness; darkness, inactivity, heedlessness and delusion (14.10-14.13). The guṇa that prevails at death decides the next birth, and each has its fruit and direction — upward, middle, downward (14.14-14.18). The seer who sees no doer but the guṇas and knows what is beyond them attains the Lord's state; going beyond the guṇas one attains immortality (14.19-14.20). Arjuna asks for the marks, conduct and means of the one beyond the guṇas (14.21); the Lord describes his evenness and non-involvement (14.22-14.25) and names the means: unswerving devotion, which makes one fit for becoming brahman (14.26). The Lord is the foundation of brahman, the immortal, everlasting dharma and absolute happiness (14.27).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Chapter purpose as the chapter states it: the knowledge by which sages reached the highest perfection (14.1), the binding of the embodied one by the guṇas (14.5) and going beyond them (14.20, 14.26).

original.text: māṃ ca yo'vyabhicāreṇa bhakitayogena sevate|sa guṇānsamatītyaitān brahmabhūyāya kalpate
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: And whoever serves (sevate) me with the unswerving yoga of devotion (avyabhicāreṇa bhakti-yogena), he, having gone beyond these guṇas, is fit for becoming brahman (brahma-bhūya).

original.text: brahmaṇo hi pratiṣṭhā'hamamṛtasyāvyayasya ca|śāśvatasya ca dharmasya sukhasyaikāntikasya ca
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: For I am the foundation (pratiṣṭhā) of brahman, of the immortal and imperishable, of everlasting dharma and of unconditional happiness (aikāntika sukha).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: amṛtasyāvyayasya may qualify brahman ('of the immortal, imperishable brahman') or name further items. The commentators divide on 'foundation' and on 'brahman' here: some take 'I' as the ground or condensed form of the highest brahman (Śrīdhara glosses pratiṣṭhā as 'image', brahman made dense); others take brahman as the state of brahman just named in 14.26, attained by the devotee, whose support is the Lord (Rāmānuja). aikāntika: 'absolute, exclusive, unfailing'.

paraphrase: Chapter 15 (20 verses) is the teaching of the highest person (puruṣottama). Movements: the imperishable aśvattha with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic metres, its branches nourished by the guṇas and its roots binding through action in the human world (15.1-15.2); it is to be cut with the weapon of non-attachment, and the place of no return sought, taking refuge in the primal person (15.3-15.4); those free of pride, delusion, attachment, desire and the pairs reach it; it is the Lord's supreme abode, not lit by sun, moon or fire (15.5-15.6). An eternal portion of the Lord, become the living being, draws the senses and mind, carries them from body to body and enjoys objects; the deluded do not see it, those with the eye of knowledge and striving yogins do (15.7-15.11). The Lord is the radiance of sun, moon and fire, sustains beings by entering the earth, nourishes plants as soma, digests food as vaiśvānara, is seated in the heart of all and is what all the Vedas make known (15.12-15.15). There are two persons, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable; the highest person, the supreme self, is another, and the Lord, being beyond both, is called puruṣottama (15.16-15.18). Whoever knows him thus worships him with all his being (15.19). This most secret teaching makes one wise and one who has done what is to be done (15.20).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Chapter purpose as the chapter states it: knowing the Lord as the highest person (15.18-15.19); the chapter closes by calling itself the most secret teaching (15.20).

original.text: śrī bhagavānuvācaūrdhvamūlamadhaḥśākhamaśvatthaṃ prāhuravyayam|chandāṃsi yasya parṇāni yastaṃ veda sa vedavit
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: The Blessed Lord said: They speak of an imperishable (avyaya) aśvattha tree with its roots above and its branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic metres (chandas); whoever knows it knows the Veda (veda-vit).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: The segment's IAST runs the speaker heading into the verse ('uvācaūrdhva-'). chandas: the metres, or the Vedic hymns. The verse does not itself call the tree saṃsāra; the commentators do, and explain 'imperishable' as its beginningless continuance. Parallel KU 2.3.1 ('ūrdhvamūlo 'vākśākha eṣo 'śvatthaḥ sanātanaḥ').

original.text: adhaścordhvaṃ prasṛtāstasya śākhā     guṇapravṛddhā viṣayapravālāḥ|adhaśca mūlānyanusantatāni     karmānubandhīni manuṣyaloke
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: Its branches spread below and above, nourished by the guṇas (guṇa-pravṛddha), with the sense-objects (viṣaya) as their shoots; and below, in the world of humans, its roots stretch on, binding through action (karma-anubandhin).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: karmānubandhin: 'having action as consequence' or 'binding (one) to action'. Besides the root above (15.1), roots are here said to stretch below, in the human world.

original.text: na rūpamasyeha tathopalabhyate    nānto na cādirna ca saṃpratiṣṭhā|aśvatthamenaṃ suvirūḍhamūla    masaṅgaśastreṇa dṛḍhena chittvā

speaker: Kṛṣṇa

original.text: tataḥ padaṃ tatparimārgitavya    yasmingatā na nivartanti bhūyaḥ|tameva cādyaṃ puruṣaṃ prapadye    yataḥ pravṛttiḥ prasṛtā purāṇī

original.text: nirmānamohā jitasaṅgadoṣā    adhyātmanityā vinivṛttakāmāḥ|dvandvairvimuktāḥ sukhaduḥkhasaṃjñai    rgacchantyamūḍhāḥ padamavyayaṃ tat
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: Free from pride and delusion (nirmāna-moha), having conquered the fault of attachment (saṅga-doṣa), constantly intent on what pertains to the self (adhyātma-nitya), with desires turned away (vinivṛtta-kāma), released from the pairs (dvandva) known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable place (pada avyaya).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: adhyātma-nitya: 'constant in adhyātma'; compare adhyātma-jñāna-nityatva in 13.12.

original.text: na tadbhāsayate sūryo na śaśāṅko na pāvakaḥ|yadgatvā na nivartante taddhāma paramaṃ mama
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: That the sun does not illumine, nor the moon, nor fire; having gone there they do not return: that is my supreme abode (dhāma paramaṃ mama).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Echoes KU 2.2.15 / MuU 2.2.10 / ŚU 6.14 ('na tatra sūryo bhāti na candratārakam'). 'tad dhāma paramaṃ mama' as in 8.21.

original.text: mamaivāṃśo jīvaloke jīvabhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ|manaḥṣaṣṭhānīndriyāṇi prakṛtisthāni karṣati
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: A portion (aṃśa) of me alone, eternal (sanātana), having become the living being (jīva-bhūta) in the world of the living (jīva-loka), draws (karṣati) the senses, with the mind (manas) as the sixth, which abide in prakṛti.
speaker: Kṛṣṇa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

The commentators divide on 'portion': Śaṅkara, a part as it were, like the sun reflected in water or the space enclosed in a pot; Rāmānuja, a real and eternal part of the Lord; Dvaita doctrine, a separated portion (vibhinnāṃśa) distinct from him. karṣati: 'draws, pulls'. original.text: śarīraṃ yadavāpnoti yaccāpyutkrāmatīśvaraḥ|gṛhītvaitāni saṃyāti vāyurgandhānivāśayāt

original.text: śrotraṃ cakṣuḥ sparśanaṃ ca rasanaṃ ghrāṇameva ca|adhiṣṭhāya manaścāyaṃ viṣayānupasevate
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

original.text: yatanto yoginaścainaṃ paśyantyātmanyavasthitam|yatanto'pyakṛtātmāno nainaṃ paśyantyacetasaḥ

original.text: yadādityagataṃ tejo jagadbhāsayate'khilam|yaccandramasi yaccāgnau tattejo viddhi māmakam

original.text: gāmāviśya ca bhūtāni dhārayāmyahamojasā|puṣṇāmi cauṣadhīḥ sarvāḥ somo bhūtvā rasātmakaḥ
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

original.text: ahaṃ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṃ dehamāśritaḥ|prāṇāpānasamāyuktaḥ pacāmyannaṃ caturvidham
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: Becoming the fire common to all (vaiśvānara), I dwell in the bodies of breathing beings and, joined with the in-breath and out-breath (prāṇa and apāna), I cook (digest) the fourfold food.

original.text: sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo    mattaḥ smṛtirjñānamapohanaṃ ca|vedaiśca sarvairahameva vedyo    vedāntakṛdvedavideva cāham
original.edition: Sanskrit text from github.com/gita/gita data/verse.json (vulgate; 701 entries incl. the extra verse at the start of ch. 13 found in some editions)

paraphrase: And I am seated in the heart of all; from me come memory (smṛti), knowledge (jñāna) and apohana (their loss, or: exclusion). I alone am what is to be known by all the Vedas; I am the maker of the Vedānta (vedānta-kṛt) and the knower of the Veda (veda-vid).
speaker: Kṛṣṇa

original.text: dvāvimau puruṣau loke kṣaraścākṣara eva ca|kṣaraḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni kūṭastho'kṣara ucyate
